title: Trump: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds
description_short: Trump: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds
description_medium: An Economist/YouGov poll conducted February 27–March 2, 2026, found that 50% of respondents somewhat or strongly supported abolishing ICE, while 39% opposed it. Support was higher among Democrats and independents, while most Republicans opposed abolition. The Guardian reported the results amid scrutiny of immigration enforcement and a partial Homeland Security shutdown; the poll also asked about ICE’s tactics and public confidence in the agency.
description_long: The Economist/YouGov poll, conducted from February 27 through March 2, 2026, found that half of respondents somewhat or strongly supported abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, while 39% opposed it. Support reached 77% among Democrats and 52% among independents; 68% of Republicans opposed abolition. The survey also asked about specific practices: 75% favored requiring ICE officers to wear identifying uniforms, 59% opposed allowing agents to hide their faces with masks, 58% said the agency used excessive force, and 44% said they had no confidence in ICE. The Guardian placed those views amid Trump administration enforcement operations and a partial Department of Homeland Security shutdown, including scrutiny of Secretary Kristi Noem after the Minneapolis deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. The results show public opinion at a particular point during the dispute over immigration enforcement. The available poll page does not provide the sample size or full questionnaire and methodology, so the precise wording and survey design cannot be assessed from the supplied information.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds

notes: The poll article gives subgroup findings and views on ICE practices, but the available page does not provide the sample size or full questionnaire and methodology.

title: Trump's Own Prewar Intelligence Said the Iran War Wasn't Likely to Change the Regime
description_short: Trump's Own Prewar Intelligence Said the Iran War Wasn't Likely to Change the Regime
description_medium: The Associated Press reported that a U.S. intelligence assessment completed before the Iran war found military intervention was unlikely to change the country’s leadership. The supplied account does not identify the assessment’s date, authoring agency, confidence level or scope, and it provides no dated Trump statement promising regime change. The report therefore does not establish that he knew of or contradicted that assessment.
description_long: The Associated Press reported that a prewar U.S. intelligence assessment judged military intervention in Iran unlikely to change the country’s leadership. Such an assessment addresses the probability of an outcome; it does not by itself show that regime change was the administration’s stated objective or that officials ignored the analysis. The available report summary does not identify when the assessment was completed, which agency prepared it, how certain analysts were, or whether it addressed the same outcome Trump discussed publicly. It also provides no direct quotation or date for a promise by Trump to change the Iranian government. Without those details, the assessment cannot be compared with his statements to establish what he knew or whether he misrepresented intelligence. The assessment’s broad judgment can be reported, but whether it informed Trump’s public claims remains unknown without the document and his dated remarks.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Own Prewar Intelligence Said the Iran War Wasn't Likely to Change the Regime
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Own Prewar Intelligence Said the Iran War Wasn't Likely to Change the Regime

notes: Needs context: the AP page returned HTTP 403; the headline supplies only the assessment’s broad finding. The packet lacks its date, agency, confidence level, scope, and Trump’s dated statements. Proposed correction: describe the reported assessment without alleging knowledge, suppression or deliberate misrepresentation until those records are available.

title: Voter Roll Purges and Mass Disenfranchisement - Federal Access to State Registration Databases
description_short: Voter Roll Purges and Mass Disenfranchisement - Federal Access to State Registration Databases
description_medium: The linked Project 2025 analyses warn that weakening federal voting-rights enforcement could reduce protection under laws such as the Voting Rights Act. They do not document a DHS rule requiring states to provide voter-registration or DMV data in exchange for grants, or a federal campaign using such data to remove voters. The alleged implementation is not established by these sources.
description_long: The linked materials discuss Project 2025 and possible changes to federal voting-rights enforcement. Common Cause warned that reducing the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division capacity could weaken enforcement of the Voting Rights Act and National Voter Registration Act. That concern is distinct from the entry’s claim that the administration conditioned Department of Homeland Security grants on states providing voter-registration and motor-vehicle records, then used those data to direct mass purges. The sources do not identify a grant condition, federal directive, participating states, database transfers or resulting removals from voter rolls. Without those records, they do not establish that a federal data-sharing program or coordinated purge campaign occurred. The analysis supports describing concerns about proposed enforcement changes, but not a completed operation targeting minority, young or Democratic-leaning voters. A DHS grant term or directive and state records showing participation and effects would be necessary to substantiate that broader account.
subcategory: Systematic Voter Suppression and Electoral Manipulation

title: Most Americans Said Trump's Iran War Wasn't Going Well
description_short: Most Americans Said Trump's Iran War Wasn't Going Well
description_medium: A CBS News/YouGov poll fielded March 17–20, 2026, found that most respondents thought the Iran conflict was not going well and described it as a war of choice rather than necessity. Many wanted the fighting to end quickly and were concerned about gasoline prices and the economy. Republican and MAGA respondents were more supportive of Trump and the military campaign than Democrats and independents.
description_long: CBS News and YouGov surveyed 3,335 U.S. adults from March 17 through 20, 2026, with a reported margin of error of 2.1 percentage points. Most respondents said the Iran conflict was not going well and characterized it as a war of choice rather than a necessity. Many said the administration had not clearly explained its goals, wanted the fighting to end quickly, and connected the conflict with higher gasoline prices and concern about the economy. Most did not expect the war to improve the U.S. economy, and a little over one-third thought it would make the country safer over the long term. Views differed by party: Republicans, particularly MAGA voters, expressed more support for Trump and the military action, while disapproval was more common among Democrats and independents. The poll records opinion during the conflict, not battlefield outcomes or a future policy decision. The poll provides a dated snapshot of public attitudes during the conflict; it does not measure battlefield outcomes or determine what policy the administration would pursue next.

preserved_fields.title: Most Americans Said Trump's Iran War Wasn't Going Well
preserved_fields.description_short: Most Americans Said Trump's Iran War Wasn't Going Well

notes: CBS/YouGov reports a sample of 3,335 adults interviewed March 17–20 and a 2.1-point margin of error. The supplied article summary does not give every response percentage.

title: Trump's Deportation Machine Was So Warehousing-Obsessed DHS Had to Pause New Immigrant Holding Deals
description_short: Trump's Deportation Machine Was So Warehousing-Obsessed DHS Had to Pause New Immigrant Holding Deals
description_medium: On April 1, 2026, DHS paused purchases of additional warehouses for immigrant detention while reviewing contracts signed under former secretary Kristi Noem. The Associated Press reported that 11 warehouses in eight states had already been bought for $1.074 billion and were also under review. DHS had a separate plan to expand detention capacity to 92,000 beds. The pause did not close existing facilities or end that plan.
description_long: PBS NewsHour, carrying an Associated Press report, said on April 1, 2026, that the Department of Homeland Security had paused purchases of additional warehouses intended for immigrant detention while it reviewed contracts signed under former secretary Kristi Noem. The review also covered completed purchases: DHS had spent a combined $1.074 billion on 11 warehouses in eight states. The department had inherited a separate $38.3 billion plan to expand detention capacity to 92,000 beds through large detention centers and regional processing sites. The warehouse purchases faced local opposition over the facilities and potential demands on water and sewer systems; lawsuits were pending in three states, and some proposed sales fell through when owners declined to sell. The pause followed Markwayne Mullin’s arrival as DHS secretary. It applied to new acquisitions and contract review. It did not show that existing warehouses would close or that the administration had abandoned its broader detention-expansion plan. The report describes a contract review and detention-expansion plan, not DHS’s motive for purchasing the warehouses.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Deportation Machine Was So Warehousing-Obsessed DHS Had to Pause New Immigrant Holding Deals
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Deportation Machine Was So Warehousing-Obsessed DHS Had to Pause New Immigrant Holding Deals

notes: The report documents a pause in new purchases and review of existing contracts; it does not show that existing warehouses closed or that the broader detention plan ended.
